items.title: Where to Connect? Boosting MLLMs via Dynamic Gated Pathways across ALL ViT and LLM Layers
items.summary: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired…
items.aiSummary: Dynamic Gated Pathways enables all-to-all adaptive routing between every vision transformer layer and every large language model layer, allowing each LLM layer to select visual granularities and improving multimodal performance.
items.abstract: A central yet under-explored question in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) is where to connect---how visual information from a hierarchical vision encoder should be wired into the layer-wise semantics of a large language model. Mainstream MLLMs inject a fixed single-layer visual representation into the LLM and treat all LLM layers as a single consumer, ignoring that different layers demand different visual granularities. Recent multi-layer fusion methods either compress hierarchical features on the encoder side or rely on predefined sparse or hierarchical layer-to-layer connections, and therefore stop short of modeling adaptive cross-layer interactions between the ViT and LLM hierarchies. We address this gap with DGP (Dynamic Gated Pathways), a routing mechanism that establishes all-to-all connections between every ViT layer and every LLM layer, with each LLM layer dynamically gating its preference over visual layers conditioned on its own semantic state. Built on top of LLaVA-1.5-7B and 13B, DGP delivers consistent gains over the LLaVA-1.5-7B baseline (e.g., +4.2 on SQA^{I}, +3.3 on MM-Vet, +3.1 on VizWiz and LLaVA^{W}) and surpasses prior multi-layer visual fusion methods on most benchmarks. Layer-wise routing analyses further show that different LLM layers do select different visual granularities on demand, supporting both the effectiveness and interpretability of the proposed dynamic gated pathways. The code is available: https://github.com/YingyingYan1/DGP.

items.title: LLMs Don't Know What They Know: Benchmarking Temporal Self-Knowledge for Financial Backtesting
items.summary: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners…
items.aiSummary: A benchmark of dated U.S. financial facts shows that large language models often understate their knowledge and that common safeguards cannot reliably certify that historical backtests are free of information leakage.
items.abstract: Financial backtests of large language models (LLMs) are meaningful only if the model did not already know the outcomes it is asked to predict. Practitioners guard against this by trusting a vendor's stated knowledge cutoff, by asking the model what it knows, or by instructing it to answer as of a past date. To verify whether any of these safeguards can be trusted, we introduce FinDendro, a benchmark of 2,226 dated U.S. facts from 1999 to 2026, covering monthly macroeconomic series, month-end stock prices and Federal Reserve decisions. Each fact yields four prompts: a value question, Recall and Predict questions that pair each candidate value with a claim of knowing or guessing without a declared date, and a Predict question with a historical declared date. Controls for persistence and dominant outcomes keep chance accuracy near 0.27. Results show that for most frontier models, self-reports understate knowledge. GPT-5 answers 76% of controlled facts correctly but claims to know 38%, and answers 61% of the facts it says it does not know. Knowledge claims can persist beyond the measured knowledge boundary, by up to seven quarters, and a declared date removes most of the claims of prior knowledge while leaving accuracy unchanged. Backtests inside a model's training window therefore cannot be certified leak-free by self-report, instruction or stated cutoff. These findings motivate behavioral measurement of temporal knowledge boundaries, and FinDendro provides a benchmark and procedure for selecting backtest periods based on demonstrated factual knowledge.

items.title: Tools Need Not Speak in Text: Latent Context Compression for Agents
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and…
items.aiSummary: A continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents compresses tool observations into latent tokens and uses action-preserving training to reduce token consumption and runtime while improving task performance.
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents typically append raw tool outputs to their context. Over multi-step interactions, long and noisy observations incur substantial context overhead and dilute the agent's attention to task-relevant information. Existing token pruning and summarization methods remain constrained by discrete text representations, limiting the achievable compression ratios. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that agents must consume tool observations as explicit text tokens. To this end, we propose Coca-Cola, a continuous latent context compression model for LLM agents. Coca-Cola compresses tool observations into latent tokens and embeds them into the input embedding space of the agent. We further introduce Action-Preserving Training, which aligns the agent's next-action distributions under full and compressed observations. This trains the compression model to learn action-sufficient latent tokens that retain decision-critical information. Experiments with web-search agents on four QA benchmarks and two model families show that Coca-Cola reduces the agent's token consumption by 70.01%-89.24% and end-to-end runtime by 24.45%-55.97%, while consistently improving task performance. These results suggest that Coca-Cola offers a promising approach for context compression in agents. Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-Agent/Coca-cola.

items.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
items.summary: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift.…
items.aiSummary: TailSteer is a final-stage training framework that reduces cumulative visual drift in multi-turn image editing by applying on-policy denoising corrections near the trajectory tail while preserving pretrained generative and editing abilities.
items.abstract: Strong single-turn editing performance does not guarantee reliable multi-turn interaction: as edited outputs are repeatedly reused, small unintended changes can accumulate into severe visual drift. This long-term drift is often mitigated through training on multi-turn data or cross-turn rollouts, potentially altering pretrained priors, or through specialized inference-time mechanisms that are difficult to scale to foundation models. We introduce TailSteer, a final-stage training framework that improves multi-turn robustness while retaining the generative and editing capabilities acquired through earlier training. TailSteer follows a simple principle: keep early denoising dynamics close to those of the base model and concentrate preservation corrections near the trajectory tail, where fine-grained deviations can be suppressed. These corrections are learned from the editor's own on-policy denoising rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference without requiring curated ground-truth editing pairs. Experiments across the FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen families show that TailSteer substantially reduces cumulative drift over 15-20 editing turns while largely preserving base-model performance on extensive text-to-image and single-image editing benchmarks. These results demonstrate that long-horizon editing robustness can be unlocked in foundation models after TailSteer, rather than by relearning their existing capabilities.

items.title: Decode Before You Hear: Speculative Listening for Chunk-Interleaved Full-Duplex Speech Language Models
items.summary: Chunk-interleaved full-duplex speech language models listen and speak in fixed time chunks, and each chunk must be processed before the next one arrives. Their workload…
items.aiSummary: A training-free, lossless speculative decoding framework drafts future audio chunks during idle time and verifies them when audio arrives, reducing response and tool-call latency in full-duplex speech language models.
items.abstract: Chunk-interleaved full-duplex speech language models listen and speak in fixed time chunks, and each chunk must be processed before the next one arrives. Their workload is asymmetric across chunks: listen chunks leave compute idle while awaiting audio, and speak and tool-call chunks require serial generation, which delays responses and tool calls. Using the idle compute for the next chunk requires decoding it before its audio arrives, under an assumed input. Taking silence as the assumed input and comparing the output with the output under real audio on four models, we observe two properties. First, the next audio chunk does not change the output in 95.3% of chunks. Second, 88% of changes begin at the first output token. Building on these properties, we propose Speculative Listening, a training-free, lossless framework for input-time self-speculative decoding. During idle time, the model drafts the next chunk under silence and, for changes at the first token, a second branch from the runner-up first token. It keeps all drafts in a cross-chunk hypothesis pool and verifies them when the audio arrives. On our eight-task benchmark TickTock-Bench, Speculative Listening speeds up speak chunks by 2.6-2.8x and tool-call chunks by up to 23.4x. On average, it reduces the decoding delay before a response starts by 73%, to 74-241 ms, close to the 200 ms gap between human turns, and the maximum lag behind real time by 94.4%.

items.title: Future Representation Distillation for Imagination-free World Action Models
items.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is…
items.aiSummary: A robot control method repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder via representation distillation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos and achieving real-time control.
items.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use the predictive knowledge of pretrained video diffusion models for robot control through future video prediction. However, iterative video denoising is costly, and inaccurate visual predictions can compromise action prediction. Our key idea is to make this predictive knowledge available through visual representations computed from the current observation, enabling action prediction without generating future videos. We introduce DreamFree, a WAM that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a predictive visual encoder through representation distillation. The visual encoder learns to predict a frozen video diffusion model's representation using only the current observation. An action module is then trained to predict actions by extracting action-relevant information from the visual encoder. Across real-world and simulated tasks, DreamFree achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art VLAs and WAMs, while performing real-time closed-loop control at 11Hz with a 14B video diffusion backbone. Experiments show that DreamFree can translate stronger video priors and additional video data into better robot control and enable learning new robot tasks from video demonstrations, including videos from a different embodiment, without action annotation for the new tasks.

items.title: Open-HumanScale: An Open Recipe for Scaling Human and Robot Experience for Embodied Foundation Models
items.summary: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data…
items.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.

items.title: D3D: Decoupled Diffusion Drafting for Asynchronous Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to…
items.aiSummary: A standalone diffusion drafter using blockwise denoising and auxiliary autoregressive supervision enables asynchronous speculative decoding by drafting successor blocks during verification, yielding large decoding speedups.
items.abstract: Target-conditioned diffusion drafters predict candidate tokens in parallel, yet each new block must wait for updated target-model hidden states. This forces drafting and verification to run sequentially, limiting speedup even though each block is generated in one pass. We introduce D3D, a standalone diffusion drafter that removes this inter-round dependency. D3D combines blockwise denoising with auxiliary autoregressive supervision to achieve long accepted prefixes without target hidden states. This independence lets D3D draft successor blocks during verification in one packed pass, enabling asynchronous speculative decoding. We progressively prune layers according to their effect on acceptance length to reduce the cost of packed drafting. Removing five of 36 layers retains over 99\% of mean acceptance length across three benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the target. Across seven benchmarks, D3D averages 5.00times and 5.71times decoding speedup with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B targets, compared with 4.03times and 3.67times for DFlash. On GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, speedup reaches 7.48times. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/fudan-generative-vision/D3D.

items.title: From Autonomous Agents to Cognitive Symbionts: Toward AI-Augmented Human Intelligence
items.summary: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write…
items.aiSummary: Physical AI should include AI-augmented human intelligence via lifelong cognitive symbionts that close cognitive gaps through sensing, context retention, and proactive assistance, requiring embedded governance.
items.abstract: For a decade, progress in artificial intelligence has been measured by how much a machine can do on its own. Large foundation models now write code and run multistep tasks, and personal agents act on a person's behalf. Yet people still forget what they once knew, miss what they are not looking at, fail to find the right words, and face hard choices without the benefit of their own history, because the machine that could help stands outside the situation. As AI moves into the physical world, attention has settled on one kind of intelligent individual, the embodied robot; we argue that the era of Physical AI holds a second kind of equal importance, the person augmented by AI. Alongside artificial general intelligence, which asks how intelligent a machine can be, stands AI-augmented human intelligence (AHI), which asks how much intelligence a machine can enable in a particular person. Realizing it calls for a new kind of system, a cognitive symbiont: a lifelong, embedded, real-time, private, low-friction, and proactive companion that senses what the person senses through external devices, keeps their context across years, models their situation and their mind, takes part in their thinking at the right moment, carries out everyday tasks with their context, and keeps learning the person as both change. We give the paradigm a conceptual core, the cognitive gap between what a person could bring to a situation and what they can hold in working memory, and organize its design space as a symbiosis loop of sensing, keeping, understanding, living alongside, acting for and thinking with the person, and growing, enclosed by a personal runtime and by trust. Because a symbiont changes what a person can do in front of others, it also raises risks of a new kind, from covert assistance in examinations to pressure on everyone to adopt it, and we treat their governance as part of the paradigm.

items.title: Sketchpad: certified exact arithmetic with a small vision-language model
items.summary: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use…
items.aiSummary: A language model with a low-rank adapter and bounded external memory can be certified exact for arbitrary-length arithmetic by checking finitely many views, and it performs multiple exact arithmetic procedures on a laptop browser.
items.abstract: Language models are accurate on most long-arithmetic problems, but their accuracy is estimated on samples and carries no guarantee for an unseen input; tool use is exact but moves the computation outside the network. We show that exactness at all input lengths becomes a finite, checkable property of a network when each of its steps reads only a bounded view of an external working memory. In Sketchpad, Qwen3.5-0.8B with a low-rank adapter executes arithmetic procedures on a rendered sheet. Each forward pass reads a three-cell view and emits one step: a digit, a carry or borrow, and the next operation. A fixed runtime moves the view and writes no digit of a result. We prove in Lean that the model is then exact on all inputs of any length if and only if it is exact on the finite set of views the runtime presents, that no finite test suffices when steps also read earlier steps, and that the guarantee tolerates bounded numerical perturbation and extends to compositions of procedures. All 2,446 views pass on the deployment device, a laptop GPU running the model in a web browser. The certified model performs signed addition and subtraction, long multiplication and division, square roots and greatest common divisors at arbitrary length. It solved 200 of 200 pre-registered problems in the browser, and 220 of 220 sums of up to 1,000 digits and products of up to 20 digits, of which GPT-6.1 Sol, the strongest of ten other models, solved 217. A symbolic runtime built on these procedures solves, expands and factors polynomials with every number computed by the model, and a multiplicative gate on the adapter recovers the base model exactly when the sheet is not in use.

items.title: claude-code · v2.1.317
items.summary: ## What's changed - Added a warning to `/schedule` when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to…
items.releaseNotes:
## What's changed

- Added a warning to `/schedule` when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
- Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
- Added `onFailure: "block"` for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
- Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
- Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
- Added `anthropic.plan`, `anthropic.seat_type`, `anthropic.provider` and `anthropic.custom_base_url` to OTel metrics, events and spans
- Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, `GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost`, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
- Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with `admin:` set, kept for `admin.identity_retention_days`, which the cost report groups by
- Added `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID`: set it to `1` on a self-hosted runner to have `claude -p` run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
- Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
- Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
- Fixed `claude auth status` exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
- Fixed a project's `effortLevel` setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
- Fixed `claude --from-pr` reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
- Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
- Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
- Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
- Fixed self-paced `/loop` wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
- Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
- Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
- Fixed `/schedule` leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
- Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
- Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
- Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
- Fixed `claude -p` exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
- Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
- Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using `--setting-sources`
- Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
- Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
- Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
- Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated `/team-onboarding` guide when asked to delete one without naming which
- Fixed Claude saying a `/team-onboarding` guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
- Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
- Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
- Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
- Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
- Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
- Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
- Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
- Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
- Fixed `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS` and `DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET` having no effect on `[1m]`, other-region and undated spellings of the default model
- Fixed `/artifacts` and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
- Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
- Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an `https://` endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
- Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an `http://` endpoint
- Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT` up to 30 seconds
- Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
- Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
- Fixed `/remote-control` answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the `disableRemoteControl` setting
- Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
- Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
- Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
- Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
- Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
- Fixed `claude -p` run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
- Fixed `claude -p` run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
- Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as `cloud_credential_error`
- Improved `/design-sync` to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
- Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
- Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example `--chrome --debug`) ahead of `--resume`
- Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
- Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
- Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
- Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
- Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
- Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
- Changed the built-in `plugin-authoring` skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
- Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
- Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
- Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
- Gateway: Fixed the status line and `/usage` showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than `CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS`
- Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
- Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with `claude remote-control` a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
- [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
- [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
- [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network
- [VSCode] Fixed the Account panel showing the plan name with a lower-cased second word
- [VSCode] Fixed file links in a Claude tab opening on top of the chat instead of in another editor group
- [VSCode] Fixed attachment chips, menus, banners and dialogs in the Claude panel staying small when `chat.fontSize` is raised
- [VSCode] Fixed `ultrathink` not raising effort for its turn or showing its rainbow when telemetry is off
- [Cloud sessions] Added a link card to cloud sessions, so you can open or decline a link an MCP server asks you to visit instead of the request going unseen
- [Cloud sessions] Changed the organization environment dialog in admin settings to the personal dialogs' short layout: each section opens from a row, and unsaved input asks before closing
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed adding a network secret for a host that already has one silently replacing it; the Add secret form now refuses and points you to the existing secret
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed new scheduled tasks ignoring your organization's default environment: the form now starts on the one an admin chose instead of the Anthropic-hosted default
- [Remote Control] Fixed the next message to an idle session going unanswered after you restart `claude remote-control`, when you sent it within a minute of your previous message
- [Claude Tag] Changed newly pasted artifact links in Slack to show a simpler card with an Open button that opens the artifact in Claude, instead of Slack's side panel

OneTrans-GSR: A Generative Slate Ranking Paradigm Unifying Reranking and Mix-Ranking with One Autoregressive Transformer
items.summary: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules…
items.aiSummary: A unified decoder-only policy guided by reward-model-based reinforcement learning generates recommendation exposure slates end-to-end, improving business metrics and reducing reranking and mix-ranking latency in a large-scale system.
items.abstract: Industrial recommender systems allocate substantial computation to pointwise candidate scoring, yet separate reranking and mix-ranking stages still assemble the final exposure slate using hand-crafted rules and specialized low-capacity models. Mix-ranking combines product cards, short videos, livestreams, and advertising cards supplied by distinct upstream business channels. Although these rules and models encode valuable domain knowledge, they are inherently limited in leveraging additional data and computation. They constrain the combinatorial space of candidate slates and determine objective trade-offs through manual tuning. To enable scalable and effective slate generation, we reformulate reranking and mix-ranking as a unified learning problem whose performance can improve with computation. Specifically, we instantiate this formulation across the reranking and mix-ranking stages and propose OneTrans-GSR, a single decoder-only policy that extends our deployed OneTrans backbone to generate the exposure slate end-to-end. During training, a reward model evaluates complete slates and guides reinforcement learning toward slate-level and long-term objectives. During decoding, business constraints are explicitly enforced. Offline evaluation shows that slate quality consistently improves as reward-model and policy compute increase. Deployed in a large-scale industrial recommendation system, OneTrans-GSR mixes heterogeneous content types within a unified slate. In online A/B tests, it improves GMV/u by 2.63%, advertiser value by 2.06%, and repurchase rate by 2.03%, while reducing end-to-end latency across the reranking and mix-ranking stages by 13%. These results mark a paradigm shift in slate generation: moving beyond human-engineered heuristics toward a general learned policy creates a scalable path for further algorithmic optimization and compute-driven improvement.

items.title: StepX-OPD: Rethinking Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation in Diffusion Models
items.summary: A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a…
items.aiSummary: StepX-OPD jointly trains a text-to-image diffusion model to acquire capabilities and few-step sampling simultaneously, outperforming sequential approaches while reducing training cost.
items.abstract: A deployable text-to-image diffusion model must hold several capabilities at once, such as instruction following, text rendering and human preference, and must sample in a few steps. Capabilities and few-step sampling are built in separate stages: a full-step model first consolidates capabilities through multi-teacher on-policy distillation, then serves as a fixed teacher for step distillation. Every full-step model we evaluate scores lower once compressed, and the second stage cannot begin until the first finishes. We introduce StepX-OPD, which merges the two stages: one student acquires every capability while learning to sample in a few steps, so frozen specialists supervise it on the states its own rollout visits rather than on a longer trajectory it never runs. Because a decomposition of the rollout's KL weights velocity mismatch most heavily near the clean end, we also regress the student's velocity on the low-noise part of the rollout. Separately, we find that capability integration makes models write prompt words into images on prompts that never asked for text, and we give a variant that lowers it. We evaluate on SD3.5-Medium and FLUX.1-dev across instruction following, text rendering, image quality and human preference. On both architectures, StepX-OPD attains the highest normalized average score among the four-step methods compared and exceeds the forty-step Flow-OPD model, and on SD3.5-Medium it trains with about 37% fewer GPU-hours than sequential DiffusionOPD followed by step distillation.

items.title: Harness-S: Learning from Sibling Harnesses for Generalizable Agent Training
items.summary: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than…
items.aiSummary: A selective harness-rescue training method uses specialized sibling harnesses to replace failed reinforcement learning rollouts and transfer their benefits into a single policy that performs better under the original base harness.
items.abstract: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

items.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
items.summary: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity,…
items.aiSummary: A benchmark of 204 visually intensive search tasks shows that even the best multimodal agents with search tools solve only 26.47% of tasks, underscoring the difficulty of linking visual evidence across search steps.
items.abstract: Multimodal agents use web and image tools to answer questions beyond their internal knowledge. Some search tasks use images mainly to identify an initial entity, then rely on text retrieval. These tasks offer limited insight into how agents connect information across images, objects, and search steps. We therefore focus on visual context management. This involves organizing and using visual information and linking it to other findings during search. Visually intensive tasks require agents to combine object appearance, local details, or spatial relations with external information. We introduce VisSearch-Bench, with 204 human-written tasks across 7 main domains and 25 subdomains. It covers Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide-Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search. Each task provides a reference answer, traceable evidence, and scoring rules. Accuracy measures complete task success, while Process Score measures the correctness and completeness of individual results and subquestion answers. Across 16 multimodal models, the best system fully solves only 26.47% of tasks, even with search tools. These results highlight the challenge of linking visual evidence with search results to produce complete answers.

# Highlights

*1007 PRs from 257 contributors.*

## New models

| Model | Type | Cookbook |
|---|---|---|
| Muse Spark Open | LLM / VLM | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Meta/MuseSparkOpen) |
| Beam-1.0 | LLM / VLM | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Reflection/Beam-1_0) |
| MiniMax-M3.1-Flash | LLM / VLM | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/MiniMax/MiniMax-M3.1) |
| MiniCPM-V 4.7 | LLM / VLM | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/OpenBMB/MiniCPM-V-4_7) |
| Kev | LLM / VLM | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/autoregressive/Kev/kev) |
| Cosmos3-Nano-Sim (Bimanual, Transfer, Auto) | Diffusion | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/diffusion/Cosmos/Cosmos3) |
| FastH3 Omni | Diffusion | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/diffusion/MiniMax/MiniMax-H3) |
| FLUX.3 Image Klein | Diffusion | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/diffusion/FLUX/FLUX.3) |
| HY-Nomas | Diffusion | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/diffusion/HY-Nomas/HY-Nomas) |
| MOSS-Image | Diffusion | [link](https://docs.sglang.io/cookbook/diffusion/OpenMOSS/MOSS-Image) |

## What's new

* DeepSeek-V4.1 on GB300 gets up to 1.5x more prefill throughput under load and about 28% lower first-token latency on 32K to 64K prompts ([#44403](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44403), [#45059](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45059), [#45107](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45107)).
* SGLang low-latency mode: the opt-in NVIDIA [megakernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-nvidia-mega) and AMD [monokernel](https://github.com/sgl-project/sgl-amd-mono) plugins run DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash decode as fused persistent kernels, for up to 44% faster single-user decode on GB300 and 75% on MI350X ([#44945](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44945), [#45450](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45450), [#44353](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44353), [#44621](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/44621)).
* MoE models such as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash and gpt-oss reach the first token 30% to 58% sooner on 8K prompts on H200 ([#43363](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43363)).
* Paged Experts (opt-in) runs MoE models larger than GPU memory on a single consumer GPU, up to 30x faster than CPU offload ([#42557](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/42557), [#45787](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45787)).
* SGLang now runs on Google TPU7x through [SGLang-TorchTPU](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-torchtpu), a PyTorch-native plugin for TPU.
* You can now serve LoRA adapters on quantized MoE models (FP8 and NVFP4) with a new opt-in LoRA engine ([#45892](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/45892)).
* DeepSeek-style MLA models running decode context parallelism can now keep their prefix cache in HiCache file-based L3 storage ([#41187](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41187)).

## To upgrade

```bash
uv pip install --prerelease=allow sglang==0.5.23
```

| Platform | Docker |
|---|---|
| NVIDIA (CUDA 13) | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.23` |
| AMD MI35x | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.23-rocm10-mi35x` |
| AMD MI30x | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.23-rocm10-mi30x` |
| Intel GPU | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.23-xpu` |
| Intel CPU | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.5.23-xeon` |
| Google TPU7x (TorchTPU) | `docker pull lmsysorg/sglang:v0.1.0-tpu` |

items.title: P^2-MOPD: Accelerating Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation via Parameter Priors
items.summary: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear…
items.aiSummary: P^2-MOPD jointly optimizes mixing coefficients and student weights under an on-policy distillation objective, enabling faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD by treating experts as parameter priors while keeping the student trainable.
items.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation consolidates expert capabilities by supervising student-generated trajectories, whereas task arithmetic offers a training-free alternative through linear parameter combinations. We view the linear combination of student and expert parameters as a single differentiable model and propose P^2-MOPD, which jointly optimizes the mixing coefficients and the student weights under the same on-policy distillation objective. Unlike task arithmetic, which stays within the span of the frozen student and expert parameters for any choice of merging coefficients, P^2-MOPD keeps the student trainable, so the experts act as parameter priors without confining it to this span. Across four domains at 1.7B and 4B scales, P^2-MOPD achieves faster and more balanced recovery than MOPD from the same initialization, surpassing its final average recovery in half the training steps. At the end of training, our 1.7B model reaches 94.7% average recovery, versus 80.9% for MOPD.

# v0.33.0

## Highlights

This release features 927 commits from 389 contributors (122 new)!

* **New models**: Reflection Beam-1.0 (501B MoE, 23B active) with its DFlash2 drafter (#62074), Yandex AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B (#57963), Recursive Flint (40B MoE, 2.5B active) (#62938), Muse Spark Open (#61879), Step-5 Preview (#61727, #63147), NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super (#62957), Nemotron-Labs Dory1.0-4B (#60149), Nemotron Parse 3.5 (#61651), MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 (#63095), Domyn Edge (#62544) and the ColUltraVBERT visual document retriever (#62237).
* **PyTorch 2.14**: vLLM is upgraded to PyTorch 2.14.0, with torchvision 0.29.0 and Triton 3.8.0 (#52183).
* **CUDA 12.9 dropped**: release wheels and images are CUDA 13.0 only. The CUDA 12.9 wheels and the `-cu129` / `-cu129-ubuntu2404` images are no longer published (#62575); use the default CUDA 13.0 artifacts instead.
* **libtorch ABI stable CUDA wheel**: the CUDA wheel is now ABI stable with libtorch.
* **AWS EFA image**: a new `vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0-efa` image (x86_64 and aarch64) bundles the AWS EFA libraries and the EFA build of the Mooncake transfer engine, for KV transfer and multi-node serving on EFA-enabled EC2 instances (#58768).
* **`vllm/vllm` image alias**: every release image is now also published under the shorter `vllm/vllm` name, e.g. `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0`, `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-efa` and `vllm/vllm:v0.33.0-rocm`.
* **Speculative decoding**: the new XPress refiner for block-diffusion drafters such as DFlash and DSpark (#54448); FLy, an opt-in lossy verification policy with 1.04-1.31x decode throughput on MI355X and B300 (#53987); DFlash/DSpark no longer reserve draft slots in the token budget, taking DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark on GB300 from 1373 to 3390 output tok/s in the PR's benchmark (#59468); quantized draft `lm_head` (`draft_lm_head_quantization`, +18% decode at concurrency 1) (#59973); lookahead block hashes so EAGLE/MTP prefix-cache hits keep their last block, on by default (#61589); and MTP drafts in the Transformers modeling backend (#61270).
* **Faster decode on NVIDIA**: opt-in latency-specialized decode on GB300 for Kimi-K3 (1.5-2x at TP8/TP16, #61867) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (18.3% faster decode step at batch 1, #61868); DeepSeek-V4/V4.1 MXFP4 experts run as block FP8 through Humming on Hopper (+9-21% decode on 4x H200, #61875); FA4 sparse MLA decode on Blackwell (#55866); FlashInfer DCP prefill on trtllm-gen with 39-48% lower mean TTFT at 100k input on 8xB200 (#62029); and decode-only full CUDA graphs under MRV2 prefill context parallelism (2.6x over eager, #62377).
* **AMD ROCm**: the default ROCm image and wheels move to ROCm 10.0, with ROCm 7.2 still published as `-rocm72` (#58761); MonoKernel decode via `--monokernel` for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on MI300X/MI325X (2.32x P50 interactivity at concurrency 1, #60731) and on every MI355X layer (#61082), and for MiniMax-M3-MXFP4 on MI355X (16.6% lower TPOT, #62712, #62994); the `ROCM_OCTAVE` 3-4 bit KV cache (4.6x the KV tokens of fp16 on RX 7900 XTX, #59774); and gfx1250 enablement for gpt-oss-120b, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 (#58800).
* **API and serving**: the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/decisions` endpoint, on by default for supported generation models (#60465, #61550); token embeddings with optional late chunking on `/v1/embeddings` (#61772, #63051, #60164); `output_mode="derender"` on `/inference/v1/generate` (#60082); a large Rust frontend parity push, including no more HTTP 500 on long conversations (#62374) and unsupported flags failing at startup (#62431); concurrent worker startup with TP > 1 (#60028); and a watchdog that dumps stack traces from stuck engine and worker processes (#55700).
* **Breaking changes**: Medusa and the MLP speculator removed (#61701); the legacy Ray compiled-graph executor removed (#61712, #62228); `--mamba-cache-mode` deprecated (#60043); requests sent while generation is paused now get HTTP 503 (#51488); the NIXL connector needs NIXL 1.5 or newer (#61032); LM Format Enforcer and `--ir-op-priority` deprecated (#63423, #63371).

## Model Support
* **New models**: Reflection Beam-1.0 (`BeamForCausalLM`) day-0 support with its DFlash2 drafter and fused Blackwell kernels (#62074, #62042), plus `beam` reasoning and tool parsers (#62052); Yandex AliceAI-Foundation-80B-A3B (Kimi Delta Attention hybrid, 512-expert MoE, 262K context) (#57963); Recursive Flint BF16 and NVFP4 GGUF checkpoints with small-batch Blackwell decode kernels (#62938); Muse Spark Open (#61879) with reasoning and tool parsers (#62207); Step-5 Preview (#61727, #62126, #62132), running on SM100 (#63147) with LoRA (#62498); NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Super (#62957); Nemotron-Labs Dory1.0-4B (#60149); Nemotron Parse 3.5 with an MTP proposer on MRV2 (#61651); MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 (#63095); Domyn Edge (#62544); ColUltraVBERT (#62237); LFM2.5-Embedding-350M (`Lfm2BidirectionalModel`, #62201); Kolibri 1 through the Transformers backend (#60827); and Decision 3.0 models (#61565, #61778) and Cloudflare Clef-Flash (#61308) on `/v1/systemone`.
* **DeepSeek-V4 and V4.1**: length-aware decode indexer block selection (about 850 us saved per step at 1M context, #61039); MegaMoE experts loaded directly in the DeepGEMM layout so `reload_weights` works (#60096); `fused_wqa_wkv` split by token across TP on SM90 (#58872); MegaAttn `wo_a` writes MXFP8 input for `wo_b` (#60118); native small-head FlashMLA sparse prefill on SM90 (#61615); FlashMLA interleaved KV layout (#61371); redundant EPLB expert slots loaded (#59611); GPU Engram tables read from peer HBM, fixing DEP decode hangs on GB200 (#62091); and fixes for Engram under PP (#62208), Engram all-to-all hangs (#62269), prefill index-workspace NaNs (#60613), C128 compressed-KV writes under PIECEWISE graphs (#59709), routed-expert rows under replay (#61643, #62652) and the updated 1017 reference encoding (#62199, #62200).
* **GLM**: GLM-5.3-Flash defaults to an FP8 KV cache (9.8% higher end-to-end throughput in the PR's benchmark, #61228) and gets mHC TileLang decode kernels on Blackwell (#62745); GLM-5.3 per-token-group quant (2.8% ITL, #60927), in-place draft decode metadata (#61873) and skipped `concat_and_cache_mla` scales (1.2-3.0% TPOT on B300, #62102); FP8 indexer WK pairs kept across `load_weights` calls, fixing thinking loops with runai_streamer (#59223).
* **Kimi-K3**: KDA RecoverSSM CuTe DSL verify/commit kernels on SM10x, with verify records moved out of the KV cache so KV connectors work (#63045); online quantization of NVIDIA projections (#62980).
* **Qwen**: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next FP8 QSA KV cache on Ampere (#60602, #60992), packed NVFP4 PLE embeddings that fit Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4 on one DGX Spark (#56273) and PLE short-conv prefill checkpoints (#61601); FlashInfer GDN prefill checkpoints for Qwen3-Next / Qwen3.5 (#60050).
* **Other models**: Cohere2MoE attention/MoE dual stream, single TP all-reduce and fused add + RMSNorm (1.14-1.36x TPOT, on by default, #62101); Beam TP all-reduce fused with norms and MoE finalize (#62366); MiniMax-M3 CUTLASS MSA decode crossover (#55838); Granite MoE as an EAGLE3/DFlash/DSpark target (#61110); NemotronHMTP sharing target embeddings (#62194); LoRA for BERT cross-encoders and token classification (#61279, #61391).

* **Transformers modeling backend**: MTP speculative drafts (#61270), fused post-top-k MoE routers (#57410), graph caching instead of AOT caching (#58918) and dynamic-RoPE CUDA graphs (#58064).

## Engine Core
* **Speculative decoding**: XPress (#54448), FLy (#53987), no draft-slot budget reservation for DFlash/DSpark (#59468), quantized draft `lm_head` (#59973), lookahead block hashes (#61589), MRV2 skipping drafts no request can use (up to 7.3% prefill throughput with DFlash, #62784), Triton split-K verify (#56148), varlen Mamba2 decode for adaptive verification (#53036), and fixes for stop-trimmed token counts (#58668), block verification randomness (#61161), MTP block tables (#61174), grammar masks (#52477), EAGLE SWA prefix hits (#62206), DFlash/DSpark Mamba checkpoint reuse (#54163) and PP warmup (#62129).
* **Model Runner V2**: batch-sharded sampling for GPT-OSS (#61257) with adaptive verification (#58466), 31-120x faster long-prompt staged writes on GB200 (#62698), encoder towers skipped on later PP stages (0.58-1.27 GiB per stage, #60238), async scheduling kept for ngram (#62521), `input_ids` on later PP stages (#61016), and memory-profiling fixes (#57926, #58243, #61509, #63431).

* **Memory and performance**: UVA-offloaded MoE experts on the sorted fused-MoE path (+7-19%, #62054); DispatchPooler bypass for homogeneous pooling (up to 10.3%, #62940); linear-time encoder cache free (#62850); sliding-window block tables null freed entries (#60767).

* **RL**: per-choice `return_weight_versions` (#61347), NCCL M2N transfer with per-parameter meshes (#60934), parameter metadata sent once (#35911), the `ParamMeta` / `iter_full()` / `iter_local()` weight-transfer API (#63256), and a silent MoE weight corruption fix with packed NCCL transfer plus layerwise reload (#62555).
* **Batch invariance**: compressed-tensors W4A16/W8A16 (#60524), GateLinear routers (#59985), online FP8 MoE (#57092), and inductor batch-invariant mode under `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT` (#61118).

## Large Scale Serving
* **Context parallelism**: MRV2 PCP decode full CUDA graphs (#62377); PCP for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with prefix caching and SWA bounded replay (#59857, #62183, #62384); FlashInfer DCP prefill on trtllm-gen (#62029); direct DCP all-to-all with strided LSE (#60373); FlashMLA sparse on the a2a DCP backend (#61285).
* **HiSparse**: direct reads of GPU-resident KV, fixing OOM with long prompts and a 3.3x slowdown on 1M-token prefill (#60417); faster host pool prefault (#60869); and P/D correctness fixes (#61659, #62739, #63827).
* **KV connectors**: NIXL 1.5 strided descriptors (#61032), sleep mode with the pull connector (#59635), mixed hybrid MLA block sizes (#61002) and GQA draft head sharding (#58471); Mooncake sleep mode over RDMA (#59625) and Prometheus metrics (#56939); MoRIIO hybrid and heterogeneous-TP WRITE transfers (#60544, #61726); streaming responses carry `kv_transfer_params` (#40186); fault tolerance extended to P/D, fixing KV block leaks (#56430).
* **KV offload**: CPU offload over up to 32 shm files (GLM-5.3 offload startup 63.6 s to 38.3 s, #59546), opt-in same-step small loads (#61961), EAGLE/MTP partial tails in align mode (#61019), lock/unlock and off-thread tiering (#58168), and many correctness fixes (#63266, #60810, #63652, #62929, #63010, #60574, #63655).
* **MoE and DP**: DeepEP-v2 fused decode globalize+align (up to 2.01x on H200 EP32, #53911); Elastic EP with an external load balancer (#43202); low-latency CPU all-reduce for DP syncs (#61767) and a DP wave hang fix (#59559); EPLB fixes for MXFP4/MXFP8 scales (#61786) and NIXL reads (#62081).

## Hardware & Performance
* **NVIDIA**: Kimi-K3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash latency-specialized decode on GB300 (#61867, #61868); FA4 sparse MLA decode (#55866); opt-in CuTe DSL MLA context prefill (#62069); DeepGEMM MegaMoE with NVFP4 routed experts (#61538) and warmed-up kernels (#60468, #61657); Triton GDN decode tuned on SM100 (#61355); GLM-5.2/5.3 low-latency BF16 GEMM on SM107 (#62843); pre-SM90 FlashInfer spec decode in full CUDA graphs (73.6 to 108.1 tok/s on SM80, #60532); `cooperative_topk` sized by row length (#62171); fused GDN MTP decode for SM80-SM90 in CUDA 12.x builds (#60896); and DGX Spark Qwen4Exp TP2 plans (#61437).
* **AMD ROCm**: ROCm 10.0 default image (#58761); MonoKernel decode for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and V4-Pro and MiniMax-M3 (#60731, #61082, #61482, #62712, #62994); `ROCM_OCTAVE` KV cache (#59774); gfx1250 enablement (#58800); DeepSeek-V4 MXFP4 indexer K cache by default on CDNA4 (up to 30.7% lower TTFT, #60834, #63669); AITER MegaMoE fixed-slot dispatch (14-15%, #61262) and shared-expert overlap (#61819); Kimi-K3 Gluon KDA kernels (#57392, #59552) and specialized decode (#60683); Qwen3.5 fused GDN MTP decode (+10-16% on MI350X, #61855); Qwen3.8-Flash-Next native W4A4 (1.9-2.3x, #60816); AITER top-k for sparse indexers on gfx950 (#61943); FlyDSL GDN prefill default on gfx942/gfx950 (#60645); RDNA3 TRITON_ATTN addressing restored (about 18%, #60084); and a MiniMax-M3-MXFP4 startup fix for very large GEMMs (#64567).
* **Intel XPU**: SYCL GDN prefill backend selection (#56835), torch MXFP4 linear backend (#51965), SYCL FlashAttention for prefix-LM text batches (#62014) and NIXL 1.5.0 in the image (#60356).
* **CPU**: zentorch 2.14.0.1 with float16 on Zen CPUs with AVX512-FP16 (#61411); MRV2 Triton warmup at startup removing an 11-20 s first-request compile (#62888); INT8 W8A8 MoE brgemm (#60740); hybrid-model prefix caching (#61805); and Run:ai Model Streamer in the CPU image (#61382).

items.title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation
items.summary: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA…
items.aiSummary: A hierarchical vision-language-action framework stores task-relevant history in explicit language through event detection and memory updates, improving non-Markovian manipulation success while reducing memory use and runtime.
items.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.

items.title: EvoMemState: Evolving Memory State for Personal Agents
items.summary: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through…
items.aiSummary: A state-centric memory framework for large language model agents represents persistent facts with relational and reasoning states to improve long-term personalized dialogue and memory-grounded responses.
items.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to provide continuous personalized assistance by retaining user information across interactions. Existing systems support this process through fact extraction, organization, updating, and retrieval, but largely maintain memories as independent facts. This fact-centric paradigm may overlook how new facts update, constrain, or conflict with earlier ones, while leaving their applicability, role, and priority for the current request implicit. In this paper, we introduce EvoMemState, a state-centric framework that augments persistent facts with two complementary states: Relational States that capture how facts remain valid and relate to one another as memory evolves, and a Reasoning State that determines how these facts should be applied to the current request. Specifically, EvoMemState consists of three key components: (i) Ontology-Guided Memory State Induction extracts Persistent Facts and constructs Relational States that maintain their validity, scope, and evolving relations. (ii) RL-Based State Evolution internalizes memory-use experience into a policy through reinforcement learning to generate a request-specific Reasoning State. (iii) State-Aware Reasoning then combines the relevant facts with their Relational States and the generated Reasoning State to guide the personal agent. Extensive experiments on long-term dialogue and memory-use benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over existing memory systems in retrieval completeness and memory-grounded response accuracy. Our code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/EvoMemState.git.

items.title: Multi-layer Indexer: Overlapping Selection and Attention in DeepSeek Sparse Attention
items.summary: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by…
items.aiSummary: A multi-layer indexer reuses adjacent layers' token selections to overlap indexer scans with attention, speeding up long-context decoding of sparse-attention LLMs without retraining or accuracy loss.
items.abstract: Sparse attention cuts the cost of long-context inference by making the attention matrix sparse: each query attends only a subset of the sequence, chosen by a fixed pattern or, in recent production LLMs, learned per query. In DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA), the attention of DeepSeek-V3.2 and the GLM-5 family, every layer is preceded by a lightning indexer that scores the whole cache and keeps the k=2048 highest-scoring tokens for the layer to attend. At long context this indexer scan, not the sparse attention it feeds, is where the decode time goes. But adjacent layers select nearly the same tokens, so a layer can attend the selection of the previous indexer layer instead of its own. This removes the dependency: each indexer then runs concurrently with the attention of its layer. The resulting Multi-layer Indexer (MLI) needs no retraining and no new weights. Its default realization changes no kernel, running inside SGLang's production decode graph; an optional fused decode kernel accelerates it further on DeepSeek-V3.2. MLI composes with IndexCache (the cross-layer reuse GLM-5.2 ships as IndexShare): IndexCache drops the indexer from some layers, and MLI hides the scan on the rest. We serve DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5 under IndexCache's protocol at retentions 1/2 to 1/32 (the fraction of layers that keep an indexer) and contexts 10K to 195K. At equal retention the composition decodes faster than IndexCache: up to 14.5% faster on DeepSeek-V3.2 and 9.8% on GLM-5 at 1/2, and 7.9% and 5.1% at 1/4, largest where IndexCache keeps the most indexers and growing with context. At retention 1/r it is faster still than IndexCache at 1/(2r) while keeping twice the fresh selections: at 128K it reaches 1.32x the unmodified model's decode throughput at 1/4, above IndexCache's 1.28x at 1/8. Its LongBench, RULER and LongBench v2 accuracy stays within a few percentage points of IndexCache's.

items.title: "PRISM" Is Not All You Need: Cross-Topic Name Collisions and Scientific Paper Retrieval
items.summary: Scientific names increasingly connect papers from different research topics, leaving readers to recover a paper's identity from context. We study this convergence in 564,861 AI-related…
items.aiSummary: Cross-topic name collisions in AI papers have risen sharply, and shared-name papers remain harder to identify even with research clues, though language-model ranking improves matching.
items.abstract: Scientific names increasingly connect papers from different research topics, leaving readers to recover a paper's identity from context. We study this convergence in 564,861 AI-related arXiv records. Cross-topic name collision grows 4.33-fold from a pooled 2020-2022 reference to 2026, compared with 1.12-fold within topics. A second sentence encoder reproduces the pattern, and name-group resampling quantifies its uncertainty. Fixed word-frequency bands locate the main increase in an intermediate-frequency vocabulary shared by many research areas. We then measure the ambiguity that remains after supplying research clues. With the same three-term query construction, shared-name targets retain matched identification deficits of 25.7 percentage points under title-based BM25 and 6.9 points under title-plus-abstract E5. Within fixed same-name candidates, listwise language-model ranking reaches 89.2% using the query and candidate titles. Topic-specific comparisons show that context resolves more cross-topic ambiguity. The evaluation separates candidate competition, document fields, and contextual ranking through lexical, dense, and language-model baselines. Source-linked cases and a portable evaluation collection make the phenomenon inspectable and reusable for scientific retrieval and research assistants.

items.aiSummary: DPDM improves agent decision accuracy by combining frozen language-model representations with a shared pretrained conditional predictor that learns from deployment evidence without parameter updates.
items.abstract: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

items.title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
items.summary: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention…
items.aiSummary: An exact tiled attention algorithm integrates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style computation, reducing memory and compute overhead and accelerating long-context relative-position transformers.
items.abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4times (2.0-21times) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128times (1.4-54times) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8times faster and uses 2.4times less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

items.title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
items.summary: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results.…
items.aiSummary: BestRand stabilizes random subset sampling for benchmark compression, reducing high-error risk and estimation error across text, multimodal, agent, and VLA evaluations at lower construction cost.
items.abstract: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.

items.title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
items.summary: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical…
items.aiSummary: Velocity Matching is a simulation-free objective for learning continuous-time dynamics that avoids long-rollout instability and numerical-scheme bias while providing theoretical guarantees and improved accuracy on ODEs and PDEs.
items.abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

items.title: Hard Sample-Conditioned Decorrelated Attention for Robust Face Recognition
items.summary: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles.…
items.aiSummary: ViT-HarDis conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty in face recognition, applying stronger decorrelation to hard samples to improve identity discrimination without architectural changes or extra inference cost.
items.abstract: Multi-head attention in Vision Transformers (ViTs) allows independent attention patterns across heads, but without explicit regularization, heads may learn redundant patterns rather than complementary roles. Correlation-based penalties encourage head disentanglement, yet apply uniform regularization across all training samples. In face recognition (FR), hard samples whose embeddings lie close to competing identities are critical for optimization and generalization. Motivated by this, we propose ViT-HarDis, which conditions attention head disentanglement on sample difficulty: samples with high cosine similarity to negative class centers receive stronger head decorrelation, enforcing specialization where identity ambiguity is highest. Experiments show improvements over both the baseline and uniform disentanglement on most benchmarks. Our analysis shows that ViT-HarDis reduces the similarity of hard samples to competing class centers while decreasing inter-head attention similarity, and that applying disentanglement only to the final transformer layers outperforms regularizing the entire network. Trained on WebFace4M, ViT-HarDis achieves SOTA results among ViT-based methods on IJB-B, IJB-C, and TinyFace Rank-1, while achieving the best IJB-B and TinyFace results when trained on MS1MV3, improving FR without architectural modifications or additional inference cost. Code: https://github.com/TaharChettaoui/Hard-Sample-Conditioned-Attention-for-FR.
